## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sujātajātaka* (Ja 269) is a narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its opening frame (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related the story while residing at Jetavana concerning Sujātā, a haughty daughter-in-law of the great banker Anāthapiṇḍika, who was also the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya and the younger sister of the famous lay disciple Visākhā [Horner 1962; Lewis & Tuladhar 2000]. In response to her conduct, the Buddha admonishes her by distinguishing seven types of wives—namely, those resembling a destroyer, a thief, a mistress, a mother, a sister, a companion, and a handmaid—explaining that the first three wicked types suffer rebirth in hell, whereas the four virtuous types attain heaven [Shyu 2008; Lewis & Tuladhar 2000]. The narrative is also cited in traditional legal literature, including excerpts in Burmese *dhammathat* digests to validate moral and legal duties of spouses [Williams 2005].

 In agreement with this, DharmaNexus detects cross-language matches between the text (§0.3–1.1) and the Tibetan *Udānavarga* (D0326) [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus finds direct text reuse between the verses of the jātaka (§1.1–3.4) and the *Nīti-gantha-saṅgaho Naradakkhadīpanī* (§666–679) [DharmaNexus].
